tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Classify an LTI system's stability, decay or growth, and oscillatory behavior from the left-half-plane, right-half-plane, or imaginary-axis locations of the poles of its transfer function $H(s)$.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Interpreting System Behavior from Poles

blocks.text: For a causal transfer function $H(s)=\dfrac{N(s)}{D(s)}$, the denominator roots are the pole locations, and the core move is to read each pole as one natural mode in the homogeneous part of the response.
To interpret behavior, write each pole as $s_k=\sigma_k+j\omega_k$ and apply this action: use the sign of $\sigma_k$ for growth or decay, and use $\omega_k$ to decide whether a mode oscillates.
Use the base case $s=-a$ first. If $a>0$, then $s=-a<0$ and the mode is decaying; if $a<0$, then $s=-a>0$ and the mode grows; if $a=0$, the mode is sustained with no exponential decay or growth.

For a complex pair $s=\sigma\pm j\omega$, this rule gives $e^{\sigma t}(A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega t))$, so $\omega\neq 0$ adds oscillation and $\sigma<0,\sigma=0,\sigma>0$ set whether the oscillation decays, persists, or grows in envelope.

Classify a full pole set by combining rules: if any pole is in the right half-plane, the system is unstable; if all poles are strictly in the left half-plane, the response is stable; if a nonzero-imaginary-axis pole exists with no right-half-plane poles, the system is marginally stable and oscillatory.

Use this as a fixed checklist in every later step: locate poles, read each real part and imaginary part, then write one behavior line for growth/decay, oscillation, and stability before moving to worked examples.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Decay from Left-Half-Plane Real Poles

example_content.example_prompt: For $H(s)=\frac{1}{s+4}$, identify the pole location and classify stability, growth or decay, and whether the natural response oscillates.

explanation_blocks.text: For this step, the cue is the denominator of $H(s)$, because its roots are the poles that determine natural-mode behavior.
The transfer function is already in first-order form, so solve $s+4=0$ to get the pole location.
The pole has real part $\text{Re}(s)=-4<0$ and imaginary part $\text{Im}(s)=0$, so it is a left-half-plane real pole with no oscillatory component.
Apply the rule from the tutorial: negative real part gives decay and zero imaginary part gives no oscillation. Therefore this mode is stable and non-oscillatory.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Growth from Right-Half-Plane Real Poles

example_content.example_prompt: For $H(s)=\frac{1}{s-3}$, find the pole and classify the system response type.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the same cue as before: the pole comes from the denominator of $H(s)$, which determines the natural mode behavior.
This is the mirror image of the previous real-pole case, so first set the denominator to zero: $s-3=0$.
The pole has real part $\text{Re}(s)=3>0$ and imaginary part $\text{Im}(s)=0$, so it is a right-half-plane real pole.
Apply the rule: positive real part gives growth, and zero imaginary part gives no oscillation. So this mode is unstable, growing, and non-oscillatory.
A bounded input can therefore produce an unbounded natural response term because the exponential envelope grows with time.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Sustained Oscillation from Imaginary-Axis Poles

example_content.example_prompt: For $H(s)=\frac{1}{s^2+9}$, find poles and classify stability and oscillatory behavior.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the same cue: read the poles from the transfer-function denominator and classify their real and imaginary parts.
Factor the denominator and solve for the roots: set $s^2+9=0$.
The poles are $\sigma\pm j\omega = 0\pm j3$, so $\text{Re}(s)=0$ and $\text{Im}(s)\neq 0$.
Map this to sustained sinusoidal natural modes from $e^{\pm j3t}=\cos(3t)+j\sin(3t)$, with no exponential growth or decay envelope.
Classification is bounded, marginally stable, and oscillatory (sustained mode), which is the boundary case between stable and unstable real-axis pole cases.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Decaying Oscillation from Left-Half-Plane Complex-Conjugate Poles

example_content.example_prompt: For $H(s)=\frac{10}{s^2+2s+5}$, find the pole pair and classify the response behavior.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the same cue as before: the denominator of $H(s)$ gives pole locations that determine the natural-mode behavior.
Solve for roots by completing the square or using the quadratic formula: set $s^2+2s+5=0$.
The poles are $s=-1\pm 2j$, so $\text{Re}(s)=-1<0$ and $\text{Im}(s)=\pm 2\neq 0$.
Apply the rule from earlier: negative real part means decay and nonzero imaginary part means oscillation, so the natural mode is a damped sinusoid.
Full classification: stable, decaying oscillatory response (bounded and not sustained).

sections.section_title: Classifying Stability and Behavior from a Full Pole Set

example_content.example_prompt: For $H(s)=\frac{20}{(s+5)(s+1+2j)(s+1-2j)(s-0.5)}$, classify stability, decay/growth, and oscillatory behavior.

explanation_blocks.text: Use the same cue as all previous steps: read the pole set from the denominator factors and apply the stability and mode rules to the complete set, not just one pole.
From the denominator factorization, list every pole: $s=-5$, $s=-1+2j$, $s=-1-2j$, and $s=0.5$.
Compute real parts and choose the rightmost pole: $\max\{\text{Re}(s_k)\}=0.5>0$.
Because an RHP pole exists ($s=0.5$), the full transfer function is unstable and the response has growth tendency, regardless of the stable or oscillatory LHP poles.
The pair $s=-1\pm 2j$ contributes damped oscillatory modes, while $s=-5$ contributes fast-decaying non-oscillatory behavior; the final behavior class is dominated by the RHP pole.
Final classification: unstable, growing, and oscillatory (with a dominant growth component from $s=0.5$).

question_entry.lesson_core_move: Classify an LTI system's stability, decay or growth, and oscillatory behavior from the left-half-plane, right-half-plane, or imaginary-axis locations of the poles of its transfer function $H(s)$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Decay from Left-Half-Plane Real Poles

prompt_blocks.text: For the causal transfer function $H(s)=5/(s+3)$, which statement correctly identifies the pole and natural-response behavior?

choice_blocks.text: The pole is at $s=-3$; the system is stable, and the natural response decays without oscillation.
The pole is at $s=3$; the system is unstable, and the natural response grows without oscillation.
The pole is at $s=-3$; the system is stable, and the natural response decays with oscillation.
The pole is at $s=-3$; the system is marginally stable, and the natural response neither decays nor grows.
The pole is at $s=3$; the system is stable, and the natural response decays without oscillation.

questions.correct_answer: The pole is at $s=-3$; the system is stable, and the natural response decays without oscillation.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The pole comes from $s+3=0$, so $s=-3$. Its real part is negative and its imaginary part is $0$, so it is a left-half-plane real pole that gives a stable, decaying, non-oscillatory mode.

prompt_blocks.text: For $H(s)=2/(s+8)$, which classification matches the pole of the transfer function?

choice_blocks.text: The pole is at $s=8$; the response grows and is non-oscillatory, so the system is unstable.
The pole is at $s=-8$; the response decays and is non-oscillatory, so the system is stable.
The pole is at $s=-8$; the response decays with sinusoidal oscillation, so the system is stable.
The pole is at $s=8$; the response decays and is non-oscillatory, so the system is stable.
The pole is at $s=-8$; the response stays at constant amplitude, so the system is marginally stable.

questions.correct_answer: The pole is at $s=-8$; the response decays and is non-oscillatory, so the system is stable.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set the denominator equal to zero: $s+8=0$, so the pole is $s=-8$. A negative real pole lies in the left half-plane, which produces exponential decay, and because the pole has no imaginary part, the response is non-oscillatory.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Growth from Right-Half-Plane Real Poles

prompt_blocks.text: For $H(s)=\dfrac{1}{s-5}$, which statement correctly classifies the natural response associated with the pole?

choice_blocks.text: The pole is at $s=5$, so the response is unstable, growing, and non-oscillatory.
The pole is at $s=-5$, so the response is stable, decaying, and non-oscillatory.
The pole is at $s=5$, so the response is stable because the pole is real.
The pole is at $s=5j$, so the response is marginally stable and oscillatory.
The pole is at $s=5$, so the response is unstable and oscillatory.

questions.correct_answer: The pole is at $s=5$, so the natural response behaves like $e^{5t}u(t)$: unstable, growing, and non-oscillatory.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set the denominator equal to zero: $s-5=0$, so $s=5$. Since $\text{Re}(s)=5>0$, the exponential envelope grows. Because $\text{Im}(s)=0$, there is no oscillation.

prompt_blocks.text: For $H(s)=\dfrac{4}{s-a}$ with $a>0$, which classification is correct?

choice_blocks.text: The pole is at $s=-a$, so the response is stable, decaying, and non-oscillatory.
The pole is at $s=a$, so the response is unstable, growing, and non-oscillatory.
The pole is at $s=a$, so the response is bounded-input stable because the numerator is positive.
The pole is at $s=4a$, so the response is unstable and oscillatory.
The pole is at $s=a$, so the response is marginally stable and purely oscillatory.

questions.correct_answer: The pole is at $s=a$. Since $a>0$, this is a right-half-plane real pole, so the natural response is unstable, growing, and non-oscillatory.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The pole comes from $s-a=0$, so $s=a$. A positive real pole has $\text{Re}(s)>0$, which gives exponential growth. Its imaginary part is zero, so the mode does not oscillate.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Sustained Oscillation from Imaginary-Axis Poles

prompt_blocks.text: For $H(s)=\dfrac{4}{s^2+16}$, which statement best classifies the pole behavior?

choice_blocks.text: The poles are in the left half-plane, so the natural response decays without sustained oscillation.
The poles are in the right half-plane, so the natural response grows exponentially.
The poles are $s=\pm 4j$, so the system has sustained oscillation and is marginally stable.
The poles are on the real axis, so the response is non-oscillatory and constant.
The poles are imaginary, so the response decays sinusoidally because $\text{Re}(s)<0$.

questions.correct_answer: The correct choice is C. The denominator gives poles $s=\pm 4j$, which have zero real part and nonzero imaginary part, so the natural mode is a sustained oscillation and the system is marginally stable.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set the denominator equal to zero and solve for the poles.
Because $\text{Re}(s)=0$ and $\text{Im}(s)\neq 0$, the natural response contains sinusoidal terms with no exponential growth or decay envelope.

prompt_blocks.text: For $H(s)=\dfrac{s+2}{s^2+25}$, which classification follows from the poles?

choice_blocks.text: The system is unstable with exponentially growing oscillations because the numerator has $s+2$.
The system is asymptotically stable because the poles have negative real part.
The system is non-oscillatory because the poles are repeated at the origin.
The poles are $s=\pm 5j$, so the system has bounded sustained oscillation and is marginally stable.
The poles are in the right half-plane, so the response grows without oscillation.

questions.correct_answer: The correct choice is D. The denominator gives poles $s=\pm 5j$ on the imaginary axis, so the natural response is oscillatory with no exponential growth or decay.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Classification comes from the denominator poles, not from the nonessential numerator factor.
These poles have $\text{Re}(s)=0$ and nonzero imaginary part, so they correspond to sustained sinusoidal modes and marginal stability.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Decaying Oscillation from Left-Half-Plane Complex-Conjugate Poles

prompt_blocks.text: For $H(s)=\dfrac{8}{s^2+4s+13}$, which pole pair and response classification are correct?

choice_blocks.text: The poles are $s=-2\pm 3j$; the response is stable and decaying oscillatory.
The poles are $s=-2$ and $s=-3$; the response is stable and nonoscillatory.
The poles are $s=\pm 3j$; the response is marginally stable with sustained oscillation.
The poles are $s=2\pm 3j$; the response is unstable and growing oscillatory.
The poles are $s=-2\pm 3j$; the response is unstable because the poles are complex.

questions.correct_answer: The poles are $s=-2\pm 3j$; the response is stable and decaying oscillatory.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Set the denominator equal to zero and solve the quadratic.
The real part is negative, so the mode decays. The imaginary part is nonzero, so the mode oscillates. Therefore the natural response is stable and decaying oscillatory.

prompt_blocks.text: For $H(s)=\dfrac{5}{s^2+6s+25}$, choose the correct classification of the natural response.

choice_blocks.text: The poles are $s=\pm 4j$; the response is sustained oscillation with no decay.
The poles are $s=-3$ and $s=-4$; the response is stable and decays without oscillation.
The poles are $s=-3\pm 4j$; the response is stable and decaying oscillatory.
The poles are $s=3\pm 4j$; the response is unstable and growing oscillatory.
The poles are $s=-3\pm 4j$; the response is marginally stable because the imaginary part is nonzero.

questions.correct_answer: The poles are $s=-3\pm 4j$; the response is stable and decaying oscillatory.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The poles come from the roots of $s^2+6s+25=0$.
Both poles are in the left half-plane because $\operatorname{Re}(s)=-3<0$, and the nonzero imaginary part gives oscillation. The response is therefore stable and decays while oscillating.

sections.section_title: Classifying Stability and Behavior from a Full Pole Set

prompt_blocks.text: For $H(s)=\frac{12}{(s+4)(s+2+3j)(s+2-3j)(s-0.25)}$, which statement correctly classifies the system's stability and natural response behavior?

choice_blocks.text: Stable, decaying, and oscillatory because most poles lie in the left half-plane.
Unstable, growing, and oscillatory because the pole $s=0.25$ is in the right half-plane while the pair $s=-2\pm 3j$ contributes damped oscillation.
Marginally stable and oscillatory because the complex poles have imaginary parts.
Stable and non-oscillatory because the rightmost pole is real.
Unstable, growing, and non-oscillatory because only the right-half-plane pole affects the behavior.

questions.correct_answer: Unstable, growing, and oscillatory because the pole $s=0.25$ is in the right half-plane while the pair $s=-2\pm 3j$ contributes damped oscillation.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The poles are $s=-4$, $s=-2\pm 3j$, and $s=0.25$. Since one pole has positive real part, the full system is unstable with a growing component. The complex-conjugate pair also contributes damped oscillatory modes.

choice_blocks.text: Stable, decaying, and oscillatory because every pole is in the left half-plane and the pair $s=-3\pm 4j$ creates damped oscillation.
Unstable and growing because the complex poles have nonzero imaginary parts.
Marginally stable and oscillatory because complex-conjugate poles always lie on the imaginary axis.
Stable, decaying, and non-oscillatory because all real parts are negative.
Unstable, growing, and oscillatory because the rightmost pole is $s=-1$.

questions.correct_answer: Stable, decaying, and oscillatory because every pole is in the left half-plane and the pair $s=-3\pm 4j$ creates damped oscillation.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The poles are $s=-6$, $s=-1$, and $s=-3\pm 4j$. All real parts are negative, so the system is stable and all natural modes decay. The complex-conjugate pair gives damped oscillatory behavior.
